module_title: More Tools for Building AI Applications

part_title: AppSync Updates, Outposts, Wavelength and SQS Fundamentals

scenes.title: AppSync for live AI application data
scenes.narration: This slide shows how a web or mobile application can receive live updates about an AI generation job. Start at the client on the left and the AppSync GraphQL API in the middle. A mutation starts a generation job, and a resolver or Lambda handler creates the job record in DynamoDB. Lambda can then call Amazon Bedrock to perform the generation. The important point is that the model may take longer than the user wants to wait on a single HTTP response. Meanwhile, the client can query AppSync for the current job status. Look at the lower three examples: mutation starts the job and returns an ID with status queued; query retrieves its current state; and subscription pushes a later status change to subscribed clients. When the job completes, the response can include an output URL that the application displays. The visual distinguishes queries, mutations and subscriptions. Queries read data, mutations initiate or change data, and subscriptions deliver relevant updates as they occur. AppSync coordinates the client-facing GraphQL interface; DynamoDB stores status, Lambda performs application work, and Bedrock generates content. Keep job access authorised so one user's subscription cannot expose another user's results.

scenes.title: Outposts extends AWS on premises
scenes.narration: This diagram places an AWS Outposts rack at the customer site, connected to an AWS Region. Look at the two sides carefully. Applications, local systems and selected AWS infrastructure can run physically on premises, keeping some data processing close to factory equipment or other local devices. The Region-side management and control plane provides service management, configuration, updates and monitoring capabilities. The connection between them is operationally important: Outposts is not simply an ordinary disconnected server rack. The lower examples focus on low latency to local systems and data-location requirements. Processing near a production line may avoid a long network round trip, while keeping sensitive records on premises may support a locality requirement. But read the caution on the slide: services and instance types available on Outposts vary by offering and Region. We must not assume every regional AWS service, every model or Amazon Bedrock inference is available locally. If a model call still goes to the Region, the architecture must account for that data movement and latency. The correct question is which components actually run on-site and which still require the Region.

scenes.title: GenAI placement on Outposts
scenes.narration: This slide compares two valid placements for generative AI around an Outposts installation. On the left, Path A keeps sensitive data at the customer site long enough to redact or filter it locally, then sends only permitted information to a managed inference service in the AWS Region. The model result returns through the application path. On the right, a different option runs a compatible self-managed model on suitable on-premises or Outposts compute, keeping inference close to the original data. Do not confuse this with assuming a managed Bedrock model automatically runs on Outposts. Now study the three decision checks at the bottom: compliance, network latency and data movement. Does regulation limit what data can leave the site? Would a regional round trip violate the response-time target? Is local inference capacity and operational support actually available? A local data-processing step can reduce exposure but does not remove the need for encryption, access control and auditing. The lesson is to choose the model's location based on data rules and performance, not simply because one architecture has more AWS icons.

scenes.title: Wavelength at the 5G edge
scenes.narration: Here the focus shifts from an on-premises site to users connected through a 5G carrier network. Follow the diagram from the mobile device into the carrier network and then to compute in an AWS Wavelength Zone. The idea is to place latency-sensitive processing close to mobile users, reducing unnecessary network travel. On the far side, the AWS Region provides deeper processing and other regional services. The example at the bottom shows a video frame handled at the edge, with preprocessing occurring near the device before regional model inference or analytics where appropriate. Think about an interactive mobile experience: extracting useful features quickly at the edge can reduce the amount of data sent upstream, while heavier model work can stay in the Region. Wavelength isn't a replacement for every AWS Region service, and availability depends on the carrier location and supported offering. The architectural decision is about placement: which step genuinely needs 5G-edge latency, and which step benefits more from regional scale and service breadth? That's the distinction this picture is teaching.

scenes.title: Choose Region, Outposts, or Wavelength
scenes.narration: This slide puts three deployment locations side by side. Begin with the AWS Region column. Regional infrastructure provides the broadest set of managed services and model options, making it the natural choice for many cloud-first applications. The middle Outposts column focuses on computing close to an enterprise's own premises, useful for local systems, sensitive data and some latency constraints. The Wavelength column places supported compute near mobile users through selected 5G networks. Look at the example inputs beneath each column. A product-description app drawing on cloud data can run in a Region. A factory sensor system may need anomaly detection close to its equipment. A mobile augmented-reality experience may benefit from ultra-low-latency edge processing. The outputs are different because the underlying business requirements are different. Notice that placement doesn't tell us whether a particular foundation model is supported there. Model and hardware availability must be checked separately. Use three decision questions: where does the data originate, where may it legally be processed, and how quickly must the result reach the user? Those answers guide the best location.

scenes.title: Why use an SQS queue
scenes.narration: This slide introduces SQS as a buffer between producers and consumers. Follow the diagram from left to right. The producer sends messages into an Amazon SQS queue without needing to know whether any worker is currently available. The queue retains the messages until consumers successfully process and delete them, or until retention expires. On the right, multiple consumers can poll for work. In the example, one consumer is active while others may be idle until more work arrives. The lower chart shows why this design matters. A burst creates a backlog, but the queue holds messages while workers catch up instead of requiring all jobs to run immediately. The processing steps at the bottom are essential: poll, receive, perform the work, and delete only after success. Receiving a message doesn't delete it. If processing fails, the message can become visible again after its visibility timeout. For AI jobs such as document summarisation, this separation protects the user-facing API from temporary worker slowdowns. The takeaway is that SQS decouples the rate of incoming work from the rate at which consumers can safely complete it.

scenes.title: SQS Standard delivery behavior
scenes.narration: This slide explains two properties of a Standard SQS queue that every consumer must understand. First is at-least-once delivery: a message may be received more than once. Second is best-effort ordering: consumers may process messages out of the order in which they were sent. The upper example uses three order messages and shows a duplicate delivery and processing order that differs from the producer sequence. Now look at the lower idempotency example. A consumer receives Order ID one thousand one, checks a durable store for that business key, creates the order and records that it has been processed. When the same message arrives again, the consumer sees the existing key and skips the duplicate business action. This is more reliable than assuming a successful receive makes duplication impossible. The panel on the right introduces FIFO queues as a separate option when ordering within a message group and built-in deduplication are required, subject to their own constraints. For either queue type, business-side idempotency is still valuable. The exam distinction is simple: Standard prioritises flexible scaling with at-least-once, best-effort order; FIFO adds stronger ordering and deduplication semantics.
